## Security

From Silicon to Spectrum: Reverse Engineering DJI's Drone Security Stack

Dongok Kim

Consumer drones combine flight control, wireless communication, and onboard computing, with much of their security hidden behind proprietary hardware and firmware. DJI has built this stack around custom chipsets, hardware roots of trust, secure boot, firmware cryptography, and its OcuSync RF protocol.

Previous research has uncovered parts of DJI's firmware, RF protocols, and DroneID, but these areas have mostly been studied separately. In this talk, we follow the security stack from bootloader to RF on modern DJI platforms.

We reverse-engineer DJI's hardware roots of trust across several chipset generations and trace how they are used for firmware and data protection. We then recover OcuSync 4 uplink, downlink, and broadcast structures from communication-processor and modem firmware and validate them against real RF captures. Finally, we trace encrypted DroneID from flight-controller generation through packet construction, encryption, and RF transmission.

These results clarify how DJI implements hardware trust, proprietary RF, and encrypted DroneID, and provide a basis for further firmware, protocol, and security analysis.

Privacy for Sale

Pascal Schärli

Demand for privacy-respecting European products is growing and providers promise "mathematically ensured" privacy through cryptography. In 2026 I reviewed several such applications and responsibly disclosed many vulnerabilities and cryptographic weaknesses. This talk compares marketing promises with reality and questions in what sense end-to-end encryption is even possible in such software distribution models.

Anonymous credentials for internet censorship resistance

michele, onyinyang, Arturo Filastò

This talk is about two applications of anonymous credentials for internet censorship resistance: Tor bridge distribution, and the Open Observatory of Network Interference.

We explain the cryptography behind both systems, and how it's used to provide user anonymity, and the open-source Rust library we built so others can develop their own anonymous access policies. Then, we will dive into Lox, Tor's reputation-based bridge distribution system, where users earn more bridges and invitations over time by keeping their bridges unblocked.

We look at OONI Probe’s anonymous credential system to establish trust in submissions while protecting privacy and build per-network user pseudonyms, without asking volunteers for accounts or IP addresses.

Finally, we're honest about the difficulties in deploying this technology, post-quantum security, and next steps.

Hello Again: Brute-Forcing Windows PINs by Exploiting Replay Protected Monotonic Counters

Christian Werling, Julian Prein, Matti Finder

TPMs let applications like Windows Hello or Microsoft BitLocker provide meaningful security even with short numeric PINs using timeouts. In our research, however, we found that modern firmware TPMs rely on an obscure JEDEC standard: Replay Protected Monotonic Counters (RPMC). We surfaced two critical vulnerabilities around RPMC that independently enable rollback attacks against fTPMs' internal state, rendering PIN anti-hammering protection ineffective on a large portion of modern laptops. To demonstrate the impact, we built a custom, low-cost SPI interposer and performed end-to-end attacks against Windows Hello and Microsoft BitLocker PIN entry. Using these setups, we can brute-force a 4-digit Hello PIN in 40 hours and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN in 20 days. Despite our coordinated vulnerability disclosures, neither vendor announced fixes.

End-to-End Encryption is not the End of the Story: Security and Privacy Issues in Signal, WhatsApp & Co.

aljosha, Gabriel Gegenhuber

Billions of people trust instant messengers such as Signal and WhatsApp because they're end-to-end encrypted (E2EE), which is a good thing, but not the end of the story. Over the past few years we've shown that the guarantees users assume their messenger provides, for example a shared view of the group conversation, can quietly fail. This talk takes you on a tour of the blind spots that E2EE doesn't cover: silently pinging any user by phone number, enumerating and censusing an entire messaging platform, and breaking transcript consistency in group chats so a single malicious member can show different people different versions of the same conversation, evade moderation, and rig polls. No encrypted message was harmed during this research.

From Finding Bugs to Shipping Fixes: Scaling Firefox Security in the Age of LLMs

Frederik Braun

In January-August 2026, LLM-driven bug discovery using models such as Claude Mythos Preview became Firefox's largest source of security bugs. Overall, security reports increased more than sevenfold compared with the previous year. Most of these findings came from our own tooling: We used our existing threat model to guide discovery and automated verification, which resulted in easily reproducible reports for hard-to-fuzz vulnerabilities, including sandbox escapes. The unexpected volume exposed bottlenecks across every step in our development lifecycle, requiring additional tooling. With this automation, we fixed more security bugs per release than ever. After being the "fastest vendor to patch" at Pwn2Own 2025, we got ahead of the attacks in 2026: our pre-event fixes forced several contestants to withdraw, and Firefox emerged from the competition without a successful compromise. However, not everything that can be automated should be. We still require humans to make the early design decisions and review our changes. As the workload increases, we must take care of the people doing the work and keep the pressure on teams manageable. This talk will share what worked for us, where bottlenecks remain and how others might learn from our experience.

Don't Trust Trusted Execution Environments (Unless You Know How to Break Them)

Tristan Hornetz

Trusted Execution Environments, or TEEs, promise that your code and data remain confidential, even when they run on a computer of someone you don't trust. When applied to cloud servers, this is awesome in theory: You can now host your most sensitive data somewhere else, and your hosting provider can't see it even if they try. In practice, however, this promise often falls short of reality. Side channels can undermine security even if your code is otherwise secure, and even the smallest bug in the underlying CPU hardware can completely compromise code integrity. Even worse, malicious system operators can tamper with the hardware itself, mounting sophisticated attacks that would be impossible from software alone. In this talk, we will discuss what TEEs can and can't do in reality, present some recent attacks from the scientific literature, and show what users can do to defend against them.

Ghost in the scope: exploiting lab equipment

Hermes

Nearly every hardware hacker has a signal analyzer or a digital oscilloscope, they're fundamental companions in any hardware security testing setup. Yet, who tests the security of the instrument itself? In this talk we dig into the software architecture of modern digital lab equipment to discover a number of remotely exploitable vulnerabilities. And yes, it runs DOOM.

5€ for the Telephone Infrastructure of 3 Countries - a Story of e164.arpa

Q Misell, Lina Lastname

What happens when someone simply forgets about a domain name that forms part of critical national infrastructure?

While investigating the largely abandoned ENUM system, we discovered that the e164.arpa zones for three countries were delegated to two nameservers: one that no longer responded, and one on a domain that had been left to expire.

It was 5€ to register, so we did!

In the process, we gained authority over the ENUM namespaces for +290 (Saint Helena), +246 (Diego Garcia), and +247 (Ascension Island). What we didn't expect was for approximately 400,000 queries to arrive at our nameservers, primarily relating to calls to US military bases.

What followed was a responsible disclosure and bureaucratic quagmire. Despite our best attempts, the underlying error remained unfixed for more than a year.

Deriving the Stars: "Decompiling" a defunct browser game through cracks in Math.random()

Astrid

or: "how to reverse engineer a game developer’s bedroom from five-year-old game logs"

Hacking Jetskis – from sea-don't do sea-doo!

stacksmashing

One day, I woke up to a simple message from a friend: "What do you know about CAN bus?" Expecting him to have car trouble, I called him and asked, "What do you need?"

Turns out the car trouble was actually jetski trouble: He bought a Sea-Doo jetski for very cheap – but it came without a key..

A quick research on his side showed that the jetski does not (like others from the time) use a simple magnet key: No, this jetski has a full, digital immobilizer system, with a digital key and "security". Unfortunately, the tools to program in a new key are unobtainium or more expensive than a new jetski - and zero public information is available on how this all works.

So we dove in: From reverse-engineering the CAN bus diagnostics protocol from an older diagnostic software, over bypassing copy protections, reverse-engineering ECU authentication protocols, to analyzing the electronic key protocol, to designing our own freely programmable key and a Flipper Zero jetski diagnostic app, this talk goes into the weeds of hacking something that I didn't even know needed to be hacked: Jetskis!

APDU Smuggling: Attacking Calypso-Based Ticketing Systems

Jacopo Jannone

Tap your transit card, hear a beep, move on. Simple enough, right? Under the hood there's actually a whole cryptographically authenticated conversation going on.

Meet Calypso, the smart card technology behind public transport systems such as Paris’s Navigo and Belgium’s MOBIB. It’s been around since the 1990s, yet you've probably never heard of anyone hacking it. Naturally, I got curious.

The result is APDU Smuggling, an attack technique I developed to trick legitimate ticketing terminals into writing attacker-controlled data to Calypso smart cards, potentially enabling the creation of forged passes. No stolen keys or broken ciphers: just a rather unfortunate disagreement between two components that should really be on the same page. Walking around with a Raspberry Pi in my backpack, I successfully reproduced the attack on two independent public transport networks.

In this talk we’ll retrace the discovery, dive into the inner workings of Calypso, figure out how the attack works and how it can be stopped, and explore what changed as a result of the coordinated disclosure.

As it turns out, authenticating a conversation and agreeing on what was said are two very different things.

Hands-Free Lockpicking: Opening Doors Like in The Movies

Werner Schober, Clemens Stockenreitner

In this talk, Clemens Stockenreitner and Werner Schober highlight several critical vulnerabilities found in dormakaba's physical access control systems based on exos 9300. This access control system originates from the manufacturer's ent

Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
inMusic, the parent company of Akai, Moog, Native Instruments, and more, has decided to embrace the modding community. In an interview with
The Verge
, inMusic CEO Jack O’Donnell said, “We’re going to provide a toolbox to the community, we’re going to provide the inner workings of, say, an MPC or Sample so that people can do what they want.” That “toolbox” includes making the code for devices like the recently teased
MPC Sample Key
open source, but also offering developers an SDK to make modifications easier and lessen the risk of bricking your beloved sampler.
While Akai is eager to see what the modding community cooks up, and has started seeding devices to developers ahead of the official release of the Sample Key, the company takes reliability seriously. O’Donnell said the company wants to “make sure that our official software is completely stable and good for an artist on stage.” He can’t have Fred Again going on stage and discovering his MPC is riddled with bugs. But he also wants people to feel comfortable tinkering. “We’ll try to give them a reset button,” he said so “They can experiment with it, and then not lose what they have.”
The company is planning to make a big splash NAMM, the annual convention of music manufacturers in Anaheim, with Creator Lab, where it will let technically curious musicians get some hands-on time hacking 22 new products from across its brands. That includes products from Moog, that might not seem like a natural pairing for vibe coding because of its analog design. But O’Donnell thinks it can be, “if we open it up correctly.” That will involve building a platform for devs to work around the analog parts of the circuit.
Other companies have also embraced the modding community. Erica Synths recently released the source code for its LXR-02 drum machine,
Polyend
open-sourced
its line of Tracker grooveboxes, and Behringer has also announced a slew of open-source devices, including a $150 clone of the MPC One called
Kick
, a clone of the
E-mu SP-1200
, the
Anima DJ controller
, the
Ignite
sequencer, and the
Polykeys 61
MIDI controller.
The change in the industry has been quick and seismic. O’Donnell said of the need to provide developers tools for hacking inMusic’s products, “I can tell you it wasn’t on our task list five weeks ago. It just all of a sudden
has
to be on a task list now.”
Of course, not everyone is thrilled.
Elektron
has expressed mixed feelings about the emergence of vibe-coded mods. The company banned linking to hacks and modified firmware from its official forums, though not discussing them generally, citing concerns about the possibility of damaging instruments. A statement posted on its forums says: “We would always warn against modifications to our firmware and/or machines that could brick them (potentially rendering them unusable), prevent future updates, affect warranty coverage.”
While Elektron doesn’t want people posting links to hacked Digitone firmware on its forums, it’s not actively trying to thwart the modding community. The consensus is there’s no going back now that vibe coding has upended the music gear world, and trying to stand in the way would be a mistake. inMusic’s O’Donnell told
the Verge,
“you can try to wall them off, which is just a losing battle one … and so we want to embrace them.”

Title: GitHub - anteloc/ldraw-mecha at v0.5.0

URL Source: https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/tree/v0.5.0

Markdown Content:
**Give an [LDraw](https://www.ldraw.org/) LEGO© model to an AI agent, get back a Blender-animated version of it.**

The **agent** will:

*   **Reverse-engineer** (infer) the **LDraw model's mechanics** from its **.mpd source code file** 🤓
*   **Study** the **discovered** mechanisms.
*   **Plan** the **interactions** between their different mechanical components.
*   And finally, turn those **plans** into **python code for Blender**, that will:
    *   **Create** the required **rigs** for controlling the different mechanisms.
    *   **Animate** them according to **plan**! 🤯

## Installation

Note

The installation process will **install** every required tool and dependency **locally** on this project repo, in order to **avoid polluting the host OS**.

However, there is a requirement of setting several **env vars** on rc files, like e.g. `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`

The installed dependencies, like e.g. Blender, are **git-ignored** by default.

You'll need **Python 3.12+** installed.

| System | Requirements |
| --- | --- |
| **macOS** | git-lfs (`brew install git-lfs`) |
| **Linux, x86_64** (WIP, untested) | git-lfs, Blender and LeoCAD required graphics libs |
| **Windows** (WIP, untested) | Run inside WSL2 (Ubuntu) |

Start by **cloning** the repo and **running the setup script**, pick the right one for your OS:

git clone https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha.git
cd ldraw-mecha
./setup-macos.sh            # or ./setup-linux.sh, ./setup-win-wsl.sh

### Installed during setup

| Item | Version |
| --- | --- |
| uv | 0.9.3 |
| bun | 1.4.4 |
| [ldraw-annotator](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-annotator-nova) | 0.5.0 |
| [ldraw-xray](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-xray) | 0.5.0 |
| [jev-rerank](https://github.com/anteloc/jev-rerank) | 0.5.0 |
| [mpd2glb](https://github.com/anteloc/mpd2glb) | 0.9.1 |
| Blender | 5.2.3 |
| LeoCAD | 26.09 |
| LDraw parts library | latest |

At the end of the setup process, you'll get a snippet with the env vars to be **added to your shell profile** (`.bashrc`, `.zshrc`, etc.), something like e.g.:

# >>> ldraw-mecha (from setup-macos.sh) >>>
export LDRAW_DIR="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw"
export LDRAWDIR="$LDRAW_DIR"
export BLENDER_BIN="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/Blender.app/Contents/MacOS/Blender"
export LEOCAD="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/bin/LeoCAD.app/Contents/MacOS/LeoCAD"
export LDRAW_XRAY_CACHE="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/.cache/ldraw-xray"
export LDRAW_ANNOTATOR_DB="/Users/me/ldraw-mecha/data/ldraw-info.db"
# export TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... # optional: Jev semantic search (jev-rerank)
# other env vars...
# <<< ldraw-mecha <<<

If you're on **VS Code** or a **terminal**, **restart it** in order to get an **updated env** with the newly added env vars.

## Usage

For **inspecting** and **selecting** one pre-annotated model to animate, open the **annotated models selector** by running:

python3 model-selector/serve.py

Then, take a look at the [Process](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/PROCESS.md) guide for a **step-by-step usage example**.

## Samples

Note

More samples available at: [Gallery](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/GALLERY.md)

Animations have been generated from **original models**, not from ai-generated ones.

These are **some samples** of animations by different agents, take a look at their **Summaries** for more details.

## 42043 Mercedes-Benz Arocs flatbed truck: the pneumatic crane on its own

*   **Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5**
*   **Original model:**[42043-1_Flatbed-Trailer.mpd](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/data/models-annotated/42043-1_Flatbed-Trailer.mpd)
*   **Context:** The model was too large and complex for fully animating it, finally I accepted Sonnet's suggestion about animating the crane alone.

[▶ Video](https://anteloc.github.io/ldraw-mecha/samples/42043-crane.mp4) · [Summary](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/samples/42043-crane.md)

**Original**

## 3625 Fabuland plane: take-off, flight and landing

*   **Agent: Claude Sonnet 5.5**
*   **Original model:**[3625-1.mpd](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/data/models-annotated/3625-1.mpd)
*   **Context:** Asked for an in-place animation, to avoid the plane moving around.

[▶ Video](https://anteloc.github.io/ldraw-mecha/samples/3625.mp4) · [Summary](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/samples/3625.md)

## Minifig movement catalog: ten minifigs, three moves each

*   **Agent: Claude Opus 5.5**
*   **Original model:** None
*   **Context:** This one is actually a **generated composition**, from several **different minifigs**, to be used as a **"howto reference"** for other agents also animating minifigs.

[▶ Video](https://anteloc.github.io/ldraw-mecha/samples/minifigs.mp4) · [Summary](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/samples/minifigs.md)

## Agent's informational sources

| Need | Read |
| --- | --- |
| The whole process, step by step, on one example | [Process](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/PROCESS.md) |
| Everyday commands and recovery | [Workflow](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/workflow.md) |
| Joint types, equations, frames and fields | [Motion plan](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/motion-plan.md) |
| Source discovery and live Blender tools | [API guide](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/discovery-and-blender.md) |
| Look boards for candidates and authored joints | [Visual inspection with ldraw-xray](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/xray.md) |
| Missed contacts, rounded transforms, coverage | [Discovery quality](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/discovery-quality.md) |
| Part families, descriptions and dimensions | [Part information](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/part-information.md) |
| Testing, clearance and evidence limits | [Validation](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/validation.md) |
| Code boundaries | [Architecture](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/architecture.md) |
| Publishing a selected working example | [Curation](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/docs/reference/curation.md) and [asset archive](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-mecha/blob/v0.5.0/examples/README.md) |

## Why and How?

After publishing [LDraw Nova](https://github.com/anteloc/ldraw-nova), a sibling project for **agentic generation of LDraw models**, several people reached out to me asking about if models could be **animated** somehow.

During the development of Nova, I noticed that **adding** some **special annotations** to `.mpd`**original** model **source files**, and then giving those to **agents**, would:

*   **Help** agents in **understanding how to build** other different models.
*   But also, in **understanding how a model was built**.

Which gave me the idea that, maybe, an agent would **also understand how a model would work.**

### Reverse-engineering mechanisms from their sources

As a first step to it, I gave **annotated models** to different agents, and prompted them to **infer (reverse-engineer)** their **constituent submodels** (see **Haiku 5.5. experiment** below).

Results from **inference experiments** were both pretty **good** and **consistent** across different agents, and I also noticed the following: **many of the submodels inferred were actually mechanisms.**

After questioning several agents about those inferred mechanisms, regarding how would they **actually work**, I also got consistent results: agents would **describe behaviours** based on the **descriptions for the parts** on a **mechanism!** 🤯

At this point, I had the following:

*   Agents would **split and refine** models into submodels and mechanisms.
*   Agents would **understand** each mechanism in **isolation**.
*   Agents would **understand** how **individual** mechanisms **worked**.

The **result** of an actual **divide-and-conquer process**, right? 🤓

Which would make **handling individual mechanisms** manageable. 🤩

### Correlating LDraw source code to a 3D model

Now, there was the matter of giving agents the **means to actually animate** mechanisms they already knew how they worked.

I was playing with **Blender MCP** at the time, and Blender looked promising as a tool that would provide agents a way to **manipulate LDraw models in 3D**, imported into Blender as **glTF (.glb) files.**

But there was still an **open issue:**

_**How to map from a refined model source code an agent would understand, to its equivalent 3D model in glTF format an agent could manipulate?**_

And the **solution** I found was:

_**Annotate the 3D glTF model's nodes with the same annotations as the source code, so the agent would:**_

*   **Outside Blender: plan on submodels** 🤔 and parts as **source code.**
*   **Inside Blender: execute on matching nodes** ✨ on the **3D glTF model.**

### Putting the pieces together 😉

Title: Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs

URL Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21375

Markdown Content:
[View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.21375)[HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.21375v3)

> Abstract:Memory enables large language models (LLMs) to use information beyond their parameters, such as past user conversations, long documents, or an agent's earlier actions. For a frozen LLM, access to this accumulated knowledge is limited to what a memory system places in its context window. However, gathering and combining relevant information needed for each query while keeping the model's context short remains challenging for existing systems. Here we introduce Memorilla, a memory system that gathers information from an entire document collection into a fixed number of query-dependent 'memory tokens' for a frozen LLM. Memorilla encodes documents (such as user chats, book chapters) once into reusable embeddings, then learns to retrieve and place query-specific information in the LLM's input embedding space. Using only 16 memory tokens, Memorilla achieves the best performance against baselines including Mem0 and MemoRAG on five of eight benchmarks spanning personalization, long-document and knowledge-intensive question answering. Notably, on FactKG, it reaches 84.33% accuracy versus 80.43% with full-context inference, while using 108x fewer tokens to represent the source documents. Furthermore, Memorilla can facilitate continual learning in agentic systems where the document count (the agent's past turns) increases throughout the trajectory. In a TextWorld environment, we show that Memorilla reduces the agent's tendency to wander between rooms it has already explored, and improves its average success rate from 18.6% with full-history in-context learning to 24.2%. Overall, Memorilla aids frozen LLMs in accumulating and using knowledge effectively across long-context interactions and takes a step towards building continually learning AI systems.

Title: Inside GitHub’s new Git storage architecture

URL Source: https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/inside-githubs-new-git-storage-architecture/

Published Time: 2026-11-05T12:23:21-08:00

Markdown Content:
Last week at GitHub Universe, we announced our new Git storage architecture, capable of handling thousands of writes per second with reads that scale on demand. Through internal testing, we’ve demonstrated the ability to support 5,000 concurrent agents working on a repository, sending 7,200 pushes per second to a repo, all while serving read traffic with consistently low latency. This new architecture is the foundation for GitHub to support agentic development for hundreds of millions of developers, and we’ve been building it underneath GitHub while it keeps running.

Over the past year, agents changed what a busy repository looks like on GitHub. In our [first post](https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/building-git-infrastructure-for-agent-scale-development/) in this series, we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation Git storage architecture: minimize coordination, and decouple storage from compute. In our [last post](https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/the-bridge-to-agent-scale-git-infrastructure/), we covered the bridge: moving 99.99999% of repositories into Azure, scoping the write quorum to individual references, and standing up virtual replicas backed by Azure Blob Storage.

We also left off with an observation: very little of a write needs to be ordered. Git objects are immutable and named by their contents, meaning two writers can store them at the same time without agreeing on anything. The part of a push that needs agreement is the reference update, and a reference update is tiny in comparison. Virtual replicas were the first step toward building around that, and the means by which we onboard repositories to the new architecture.

The rest of the architecture builds on that observation. Only reference updates need agreement. That lets the parts of Git infrastructure that used to be tightly coupled (storing data, serving requests, and maintaining repositories) scale independently. For developers, Git stays Git: they push, fetch, and branch the same way, with the same protections in place. Below, we walk through the requirements behind the design, follow a request through the system, and dive deep into two of its components.

## Building for agent scale

We think about the scale of the GitHub platform along two axes:

1.   **Horizontal scale** is how many developers and agents can work across many repositories. Many of GitHub’s current approaches on this axis have been battle-tested over the years and are carried forward to the new architecture: partitioning of tenants across infrastructure, isolation and/or fairness enforcement of tenant traffic, and load-aware routing, to name a few.
2.   **Vertical scale** is how many developers and agents can work on **one** repository. As agents write more code, we expect individual repositories to get larger and busier, so most of our requirements came from the vertical axis.

Today, the busiest repositories on GitHub.com receive at most dozens of writes in a single second, typically in short bursts. As more of that work shifts to agents running in parallel and around the clock, we expect those bursts to become a sustained rate within the next year. Each push leads to more reads: CI runs, deployment systems pull the new commit, and other agents fetch it for context. This read fan-out results in a large amplification effect on overall traffic that scales with writes.

We’re already seeing this trend play out on repositories at the top of the curve. The chart below shows daily requests to one repository on GitHub from March to May, when its traffic grew about 4x. Its growth has continued on an exponential trajectory since then.

We have to plan for a world where agent-driven development keeps accelerating at this speed. Instead of planning for the next increment, we set a target of at least two orders of magnitude more scale. For a single repository, that meant the new architecture needed to:

*   Accept thousands of writes per second.
*   Support multiple writer nodes. There are two reasons for this:
    *   Experience has taught us that indexing incoming packs and checking object connectivity are the most CPU-expensive parts of a write, and that cost scales with the size of the write, so a single node will become compute-bound quickly.
    *   Spreading that work across many nodes improves fault tolerance and shortens recovery when a node fails.

*   Minimize commit latency. An agent waits on each push before it moves to its next step.
*   Record changes in order for each reference with the ability to quickly linearize across references. A virtual replica that falls behind needs to catch up by downloading _only_ the data it needs to serve the incoming request.
*   Keep reads cheap when nothing has changed, which is the common case given the read-to-write ratio.
*   Let each component scale independently.

On top of that, the system had to be able to improve overall reliability and scale globally.

## Introducing “Project Rubicon”

In May of 2026, hot on the heels of the initial Azure migration, we started working on a design that could meet those demands. We tried several approaches. In all of them, pack data lived in Azure Blob Storage, and in some we experimented with keeping reference state there too. We’ll cover some of the trade-offs we found below, but we settled on a design we felt maximized throughput while preserving the correctness, durability, availability, and latency guarantees a platform like GitHub requires. We called it “Rubicon,” a nod to the point of no return the industry crossed with agentic development.

Let’s walk through Rubicon from the top down. Many things stay the same: requests from Git clients, the API, and the web UI arrive at Spokes, which still handles routing and load balancing, and serves the internal API that the rest of GitHub uses to read and write repository data. Spokes also maintains its role as a placement and balancing service, maintaining the partitioning, isolation, and tenant fairness required for horizontal scale. The data plane underneath Spokes, in contrast, is new.

Spokes routes each request to one of a small group of virtual replicas assigned to that repository. Virtual replicas are a single fleet of disposable compute that serves reads, writes, or both. A virtual replica’s local disk is a cache that can be rebuilt at any time.

Spokes routes a repository’s traffic to the same virtual replicas when it can, which keeps their caches warm and latency low, but nothing about correctness depends on a request landing on any particular virtual replica. When a virtual replica goes away, the repository’s other virtual replicas keep serving, and a replacement fills its cache as traffic arrives.

When a repository gets busy, we add more virtual replicas. Separately, a fleet of compaction nodes works in the background, directly against Blob Storage and Ref-CAS, to merge each repository’s packs and remove unreachable objects. That work never runs on a virtual replica, meaning their CPU and memory can be almost entirely dedicated to serving requests.

Durable state lives in two places:

1.   **Git objects**, in the form of packs and auxiliary read acceleration data, live in Azure Blob Storage.
2.   **References** and the list of packs that make up the repository (the pack manifest) live in a separate replicated log service we call Ref-CAS (for “Reference Compare-and-Swap”).

Let’s walk the architecture from the perspective of a write and a read:

*   **Write:** a virtual replica indexes the incoming pack and uploads it to Blob Storage, then commits one transaction to Ref-CAS that lists the pack in the manifest and updates the references. Later, a compaction node merges that pack with others to keep reads fast.
*   **Read:** a virtual replica checks its reference version with Ref-CAS, pulls the packs it needs from Blob Storage into its cache, and serves the read from there.

There are many distinct approaches we’ve taken within the new architecture, from the software stack on the virtual replicas to how traffic routing and workload scheduling are tuned for different use cases (e.g., many small repos vs. one large one). Let’s dive deep into two components of the architecture and tell their stories centered on the two design principles.

## Minimizing coordination: mutating reference state at high throughput

Object storage services like Azure Blob Storage are incredibly good at what they do, and natural fits for many data-heavy applications like source code storage. They are durable and replicated, hold as much as we need them to, have a relatively low cost per byte, and deliver exceptionally high aggregate throughput so long as traffic is spread across many keys. As a result, nearly everything durable in the new Git storage architecture lives in Azure Blob Storage, including:

*   Packs and indexes written by pushes, compaction, and garbage collection.
*   Various read accelerators (like multi-pack indexes, reachability bitmaps, and some custom formats) that our maintenance process builds from those packs.
*   Records that let compaction and garbage collection resume or audit their work, along with the leases that compaction nodes use to claim work.
*   Cached responses for frequently repeated fetches.
*   Checkpoints for the reference state of the repository, though not the authoritative state used to serve requests.

Most of that data is written once to a distinct key and never changes afterward, which is what makes it highly suitable for Blob Storage.

References are the opposite. A busy repository’s references are a relatively small piece of state that many writes race to update at the same time. That access pattern is harder to serve from Blob Storage, and our first prototypes showed us why. Object storage for this kind of workload is an intuitive choice, and one that works well up to a certain level of scale: conditional writes give a compare-and-swap for free, and the data is already durable and replicated. However, we ran into a difficult set of choices, illustrated below by two approaches we tried.

Our **first approach** was a write-ahead log for all of a repository’s references, indexed by a single blob. Every update is a conditional write against that blob. It’s correct, and reads are cheap: a virtual replica asks whether the blob has changed, and if it hasn’t, it’s done. Writes are where it falls short. Only one conditional write to a blob can be in flight at a time, so even when we batch every push that arrives during a write into the next one, the repository’s write ceiling is one write per round trip to a single blob. In practice, this netted us write throughput in the mid-hundreds per second.

Our **second approach** split the references across several segment blobs, with each reference hashing to one of them. Writes to references in different segments no longer wait on each other, which raises the ceiling. But a read now has to check every segment to know whether anything changed, and it’s only as fast as the slowest segment. We’d traded write latency for read latency, and reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude. We can visualize this by showing multiple writes and a read side by side:

Neither option met every requirement, so we built something else: a replicated log service dedicated to references, or the Ref-CAS service. This is the (small) consensus group we said at the end of the [last post](https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/the-bridge-to-agent-scale-git-infrastructure/) was still somewhere in the stack. Here’s how it works.

Title: Scamwich: Inside a Restaurant Delivery Payment-Skimming Campaign — InfoHawk News

URL Source: https://www.infohawk.com/news/2026-11-05-scamwich-restaurant-skimming

Markdown Content:
Source: jarrysaymlckess[.]delivery and dawechlckhort[.]delivery

When customers order food online, they expect a familiar experience: find their restaurant, choose their meal, and pay. Increasingly, criminals are exploiting that familiarity by creating convincing clones of restaurant ordering websites, right down to the original site's underlying code.

In early November 2026, InfoHawk researchers investigated a collection of suspicious websites that appear to be part of one or more coordinated restaurant impersonation and payment-skimming operations.

Across two research passes, we identified 820 domains impersonating 35 restaurant brands. Of those, 808 use the `.delivery` top-level domain, and the rest use `.com` or `.shop`.

The scale is concerning, but what makes these sites particularly dangerous is how convincing they can be.

## These aren't ordinary fake websites

The investigation began with a suspicious domain: `mlckessejersstey[.]delivery`.

The site impersonated Jersey Mike's, the popular sandwich chain, and reproduced its online ordering experience.

Rather than simply displaying a crude imitation of the restaurant's website, the attackers used a more sophisticated approach: reverse-proxying the legitimate site while replacing the checkout payment form with a malicious one.

A reverse proxy can retrieve content from a legitimate website and present it to visitors under a different domain. This allows an attacker-controlled site to display genuine pages and assets while selectively modifying the parts of the experience that matter to the attacker.

In this case, the malicious checkout requested credit card information and also asked customers for the SMS verification code sent by their bank.

This is a particularly dangerous combination. Capturing a credit card number is valuable to criminals; obtaining a one-time verification code could also help them authorize fraudulent transactions, depending on how the victim's bank uses that code.

For consumers, the experience can appear nearly indistinguishable from ordering directly from the restaurant. The site looks familiar, the menu and ordering flow can behave normally, and the fraudulent payment form appears at the moment a customer expects to pay.

Importantly, this does not require the legitimate restaurant's website to have been hacked. The attackers can operate on infrastructure they control while using the authentic restaurant website as the source of the content they display.

## Impersonated brands

Mostly `.delivery` typosquats, plus a few look-alike `.com` and `.shop` names, found across two research passes. "Seen" is the range of registration or scan dates we have for a brand's domains, all in 2026. Open a brand to see its domains.

Title: Ozempic-style drugs are now in trials for heart failure, addiction and even aging

URL Source: https://maccus.fr/en/ozempic-drugs-trials-beyond-diabetes/

Published Time: 2026-11-06T09:15:26+01:00

Markdown Content:
The diabetes drugs that became weight-loss blockbusters are now in human trials for heart failure, addiction, Alzheimer’s and even the biology of aging. Most of that research is still about diabetes and weight, about five in six of the trials. The change is how fast the rest is growing.

These are among the best-selling medicines in the world right now. Where they are tested next is a question about a great deal of money and a great many patients. So I went looking for how far the class has actually spread, in the one place that records it before any [marketing](https://maccus.fr/en/ozempic-drugs-trials-beyond-diabetes/#) does: the register where a trial is filed when it begins.

Marketing d'influence

I went through ClinicalTrials.gov, the United States trial registry, and pulled every registered human study of a GLP-1 or incretin drug, the class that includes Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro. That comes to at least eighteen hundred trials. I sorted each one by the disease it set out to treat, counted them by the year they began, and took 2026 only up to this week.

Voir plus

Agence Marketing SEO

Audit SEO gratuit

Marketing d'influence

## The reach past diabetes keeps widening

Fifteen years ago this barely happened. Of the new trials starting in the class back then, about one in fourteen aimed at anything other than diabetes, weight or cholesterol.

Chart: MACCUS, data from ClinicalTrials.gov, November 6, 2026.

Today it is about one in four, and the line is still climbing.

Across those fifteen years the share aimed past diabetes and weight has roughly tripled. It is still a minority of the work, and a fast-growing one. The yearly figures jump around, so the chart is best read a decade at a time, not a year at a time.

## The biology goes well beyond blood sugar

These drugs copy a gut hormone that blunts appetite, and the receptors it acts on sit all through the body: in the pancreas, the brain, the heart, the gut and the kidneys. A drug built to lower blood sugar keeps turning up effects in places its makers did not plan for. The commercial pull runs the same way: once a medicine becomes the best-selling product in its field, every company and every academic lab has a reason to find the next disease it might treat. Both forces push the same way, which is why the reach shows up as a broad fan of diseases rather than one careful step after another.

## The map runs from the heart to the brain

Fifteen separate disease areas turn up among the trials that began since 2024 and left diabetes and weight behind completely. Addiction leads, with studies testing whether the drugs quiet cravings for alcohol and other substances. Behind it come the heart, the kidneys, the liver and cancer. A single class of medicine is being aimed at much of the body at once, the way [one new method can spread across an entire field](https://maccus.fr/en/ai-written-code-github/) once it starts to work.

Chart: MACCUS, data from ClinicalTrials.gov, November 6, 2026.

The individual studies make the spread concrete. The US Department of Veterans Affairs is testing semaglutide, the drug sold as Ozempic, against alcohol use disorder. Imperial College London is trying it on Alzheimer’s disease. A research institute in New York is running a trial against biological aging itself. A university hospital in the Netherlands is studying it in heart failure, and a hospital in China is testing a related drug in MASH, a fatty-liver disease with no approved cure. Most of these have reached mid-stage testing, well past the first-in-human stage.

Voir plus

Stratégie marketing numérique

Booster ventes

Chart: MACCUS, data from ClinicalTrials.gov, November 6, 2026.

The addiction trials are the ones that make people reread the line. The drugs dull the reward that eating gives, and early signals suggest they may dull other rewards too. A shot meant to steady blood sugar is now being tried on heavy drinking and on cravings for stimulants. A veteran in the government trial is not enrolled for his weight. He is there to find out whether a weekly injection can make the next drink easier to turn down, something no pill has done reliably. That is a long way from a diabetes clinic.

## No one planned this

Nobody set out to turn a diabetes drug into a treatment for much of medicine. Each research group had a plausible reason to try one: a signal in the brain here, a hint in the kidney there, a hospital with patients and a hypothesis. The pull to test is the same one that [reshapes an industry once the economics shift](https://maccus.fr/en/china-gasoline-car-sales/) under it. Each of those choices was reasonable on its own. Together they aim one drug class at an unusually wide stretch of human disease, with no one deciding that it should.

## What it means

The pipeline is now far wider than the label on the box, and that is the part worth watching. A registered trial records an intention to study, and it proves nothing on its own. Most drug trials fail, and most of these will too. ClinicalTrials.gov is the American registry, so studies that run only in Europe or China are undercounted here, and the real spread is wider than my count.

For a European reader the second-order point is the one to sit with: the diseases that get a shot at a new treatment are being chosen, in large part, inside an American drug industry and its trial system. The direction is not subtle, and it rhymes with how [a frontier moves once one bet pays off](https://maccus.fr/en/china-humanoid-robots/), fast and across a whole field at once.

If the share keeps climbing, the first approval of one of these drugs for a disease with nothing to do with blood sugar lands before the decade is out. The heart or the liver is the most likely place, where the trials are furthest along. These drugs already do more than treat diabetes. The open question now is how much of medicine they end up touching.
